newsitem.title: USA: Lazard says recent yield burning study "distorted".
newsitem.headline: Lazard says recent yield burning study "distorted".

text.p: Attorneys for Lazard Freres & Co told top brass at the U.S. Treasury Department that a recent study charging that "yield burning" was pervasive from 1990 to 1995 in the municipal bond industry was loaded with serious errors and "distorted."

Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, outside counsel to Lazard Freres, slammed the study by the Washington, D.C.-based law firm Phillips & Cohen in a 43-page memorandum to Donald Lubick, Treasury's acting assistant secretary for tax policy.
John Phillips, a partner at Phillips & Cohen, was unavailable for comment.
Yield burning refers to allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Tresuries bought in the open market and used in bond refinancing deals.
In April 1995, the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority filed a $14 million lawsuit against Lazard Freres, in the first court challenge to the alleged Wall Street overcharges.

Phillips & Cohen, the county's lawyers, commissioned a study by Babson College Professor Steven Feinstein, which concludes that from 1990 through 1995 Wall Street conducted a pervasive yield burning scheme involving at least 80 percent of advance refundings and nearly $1 billion in losses to the U.S. Treasury.

But Wachtell Lipton lawyers Lawrence Pedowitz and John Savarese said in a three-page letter accompanying Lazard Freres' analysis, that Feinstein's study is "riddled with analytical flaws and cannot withstand close analysis,"
Wachtell Lipton said it agrees "wholeheartedly" with a recent Public Securities Association position that the Feinstein study is "fundamentally flawed."
Lazard Freres' lawyers said Feinstein's allegation that 80 percent of all municipal escrow transactions were fraudulent is "entirely unsupported" by existing data.
"This percentage appears simply to have been made up to generate headline-grabbing (charges)," Wachtell Lipton said.
Wachtell Lipton also said Feinstein improperly relies on end-of-day spot prices published in the Wall Street Journal, which have "inherent limitations."
The law firm also challenged Feinstein's claim that there are no differences between competitive and negotiated escrows that justify differences in dealer markups.

"Informed and sophisticated municipal issuers have chosen negotiated over competitive transactions for a variety of sound ... reasons," including the fact that they can make "last-minute, market-sensitive adjustments on the trade date," Wachtell Lipton said.
Wachtell Lipton said Phillips & Cohen is dead wrong when it says the federal government can bring actions against Wall Street firms using the federal False Claims Act.
"The remedy is simply not available as a matter of law," Wachtell Lipton said.
Wachtell Lipton also sent the memo to IRS Commissioner Margaret Richardson and Loretta Finger, attorney-advisor in IRS's office of associate chief counsel.
